---
title: "Fix It"
---

Three problems have come up across the course this week. None of them mean you did anything
wrong, and none of them mean your computer is broken. Each one below has what you would see,
what to do about it, and how to tell it worked.

The first one applies to everybody. The other two only matter if you have actually run into
them.

---

## 1. Do this one even if nothing looks broken

**What you might see:** you click **Run Cell** above a grey code box, and strange characters
appear around your code in the console, something like `[200~` and `[201~`. Or the next cell
you run comes out stuck onto the previous one and both run at once. Or the console just
behaves oddly and you cannot say why.

**Why:** your course folder came with one setting switched on that should have been off. It
tells VS Code to send code in a format a different R console understands, and the plain R
console we use does not. The setting was wrong in the course template until 8 September, so
everyone who set up their workspace before then has it.

**What to do:**

1. Open Settings. Hold `Ctrl` and press `,` on Windows, or hold `Cmd` and press `,` on a Mac.
2. At the top of the Settings page there are tabs: **User** and **Workspace**. Click
   **Workspace**. This matters. Workspace is the tab holding the settings that arrived with
   your course folder.
3. In the search box at the top, type `bracketed`.
4. One result appears, **R: Bracketed Paste**, with a tick box. **Untick it.**
5. Close the Settings tab. There is nothing to save; VS Code saves it for you.

Now give yourself a clean console, because R may still be waiting halfway through a command
it never finished. Find the terminal panel at the bottom of VS Code and click the bin icon to
close it. The next time you run a cell, a fresh one opens.

**How to tell it worked:** run a cell. Your code appears in the console with nothing extra
wrapped around it, and it runs on its own rather than dragging the previous cell along.

---

## 2. "Git: Clone" is not in the Command Palette

**What you would see:** you press `Ctrl+Shift+P` (or `Cmd+Shift+P` on a Mac), type
`Git: Clone`, and it is not on the list at all. Not greyed out. Just absent.

**Why:** VS Code hides that command when it cannot find Git on your computer. Nine times in
ten Git is installed perfectly well, but VS Code was already open when you installed it. VS
Code checks for programs once, when it starts, so anything installed while it was running
stays invisible to it.

**What to do, in this order:**

1. **Quit VS Code completely, then open it again.** On Windows, close every VS Code window.
   On a Mac, press `Cmd+Q`, because closing the window leaves VS Code running. Do not use
   **Reload Window**; it is not the same thing and will not fix this.
2. Look for the command again. For most people it is now there and you are done.
3. Still missing? Check whether Git is really installed. In VS Code open **Terminal, New
   Terminal** and type `git --version`. A version number means Git is fine.
4. **On Windows,** if that says Git is not recognised, run the Git installer again from
   [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com/downloads). On the page asking about your PATH, choose
   the **middle** option, *Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software*. The
   Git Bash only option hides Git from VS Code.
5. **On a Mac,** if that says Git is not recognised, open Terminal and run `git --version`.
   A box may offer to install the developer tools. Click **Install** and wait for it to
   finish, then quit and reopen VS Code.

**If you need to get on with your work right now,** you do not have to wait for the palette.
In a terminal inside VS Code, move to the folder where you want your project and run
`git clone` followed by the address you copied from GitHub. That does exactly what the menu
command does.

**How to tell it worked:** `Git: Clone` appears in the Command Palette when you type it.

---

## 3. R says there is no package called 'v2v'

**What you would see:** the install seemed to work, with a long list of packages reporting
success, and then `library(v2v)` answers `there is no package called 'v2v'`. Looking back up
the output there are lines saying `Warning: cannot remove prior installation of package` and
`Warning: restored`.

**Why:** during the install R offered to update a long list of other packages, and choosing
**All** causes this. Some of those packages were in use by R at that moment, and Windows will
not replace a file that is already open. Those packages quietly went back to the version you
had, and the course package then refused to build because one of them was too old. The word
`restored` in that output means *put back*, not *repaired*. This mainly affects Windows.

**If your setup check came back green, ignore this section.** Nothing is wrong.

**What to do:**

1. **Quit VS Code completely.** This is the step that matters, because VS Code is what was
   holding those files open. On a Mac use `Cmd+Q`.
2. Open R on its own. On Windows, open the Start menu and look for **R x64**. On a Mac, open
   the **R** application from your Applications folder.
3. In that R window, run this line and let it finish:

   ```r
   install.packages(c("rlang", "cli", "curl", "xfun", "fs"))
   ```

4. Then run this one. The ending matters, so copy the whole line:

   ```r
   remotes::install_github("AURA-Lab-SIUE/v2v-r", upgrade = "never")
   ```

   `upgrade = "never"` is what stops R offering that list again.

5. Then check it loaded:

   ```r
   library(v2v)
   setup()
   ```

6. Close R and reopen VS Code.

**How to tell it worked:** `library(v2v)` returns without complaint, and `setup()` prints
green ticks down the **Required R packages** list.
